title: Evaluating the Veteran Connection Programme: supporting veterans' mental health through social connections
official: Assessing feasibility and acceptability of the Veteran Connection Programme (and trial), designed to enhance mental health amongst military veterans through social connectedness
summary:
Background and study aims
Many service-members struggle when they leave the military. They lose their career, their team, and who they were as a person. This is worse for those leaving with injuries or mental health problems. Many end up drifting for years, trying to find a new identity, and unsure who to reach out to. This can lead to problems like feeling lonely and depressed. Some feel constantly worried and start drinking too much to cope. 

16,000 people leave the UK military each year, costing the government more than £110 million every year. At present, most support for veterans helps with finding jobs and housing. But this support doesn't help them do well in their new job. And what's worse, it doesn’t help them to feel less lonely and find their place in society.

It has been found that being part of groups helps people during difficult life changes. That is because groups give meaning and purpose. Groups offer belonging and help people build a stronger sense of self. Because of this, the Veteran Connection Programme (VCP) was created. VCP is run in groups so people can share their experiences and learn from each other. It is delivered by trained veterans and psychologists in a safe environment.  

VCP has already been tested with 34 veterans, showing promising results. Veterans in the programme felt healthier and happier and less lonely. Many said they felt more confident and more willing to talk about difficulties. For example: “I’m not by myself anymore… I’m not abnormal. This is okay…”; “[During VCP, we] were vulnerable, which you don't usually see […] that's the strength of the programme.”.

This study will research whether VCP works, takes pressure off the NHS, and can be delivered in the right way.

Who can participate?
Adult diverse veterans and service-people who will become veterans in the next six months. This will include women, people from different racial backgrounds, people living in rural areas, and people who left the military early.

What does the study involve?
Half of the participants will get VCP. The other half will get a leaflet with support options. Participants will ask  if VCP works for them, and how it can be made better. This research also want to find out if our plans to deliver it are practical and if VCP saves the NHS money. These results will help us plan a bigger research project that will test whether VCP improves veterans’ lives.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
The benefits for participants who complete VCP will be increased knowledge about the value of group memberships for health and wellbeing. Possible risks of participating are minimal but could involve participants experiencing difficult emotions/thoughts. The researchers have put measures in place to prevent harm, including screening, signposting, and additional support measures.

Where is the study run from?
VCP workshops will be run in four locations in England: Merriott (Somerset), Plymouth (Devon), Penryn (Cornwall), and Catterick (North Yorkshire). Other parts of the study (i.e., the pre-workshop induction, post-workshop check-in session, interviews, and surveys) will all take place online. 

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
October 2026 to May 2027. 

Who is funding the study?
The Research for Patient Benefit (RfPB) stream of the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), UK.

Who is the main contact?
Dr Stefan Schilling, University of Exeter, s.schilling@exeter.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Aged 18+ until 55 (standard retirement age for most military personnel)
2. Currently serving or having served in the UK Regular Armed Forces
3. In resettlement (6 months prior to leaving the military) up until 10 years post-service
4. Able and willing to attend a face-to-face one-day group workshop and two brief virtual sessions
5. Have sufficient English proficiency to participate in group discussions and complete study assessments
6. Able to provide informed consent
Exclusion criteria:
1. Currently receiving intensive or crisis mental-health care (e.g., hospitalisation/acute risk-management)
2. In the military but not in resettlement (i.e., not within 6 months of leaving)
3. Experiencing unmanaged severe mental illness (e.g., personality disorder/psychosis/bipolar disorder/moderate to severe suicide risk) or significant cognitive impairment that would prevent group participation
4. Pose a current unmanaged risk to others (based on self-report and/or referrer indication).
